title: Bank of America’s unique take on Apple stock as Ternus takes reins
detail:
Bank of America’s unique take on Apple stock as Ternus takes reins
Celine Provini
Wed, September 9, 2026 at 11:47 AM CDT 4 min read
AAPL
BAC
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Wall Street rarely changes its mind about a stock on the day a new phone gets announced. The number an analyst publishes is a bet on earnings two or three years out, and a keynote does not move that math on its own.

That's why analyst notes pile up in the days before an Apple launch. Firms restate where they stand, walk investors through what they expect on stage, and save the real estimate revisions for the quarter that follows.

Bank of America filed its note on Sept. 8. The rating and the target did not move. What sits underneath them did, however, and that's the part worth reading.

Why Apple launch events rarely move the stock the way investors expect

Apple (AAPL) shares closed at $316.22 on Sept. 8, down 1.17% on the session, according to StockAnalysis.com. That leaves the stock roughly 8% below the 52-week high of $344.57 it set in late July, with a market value near $4.61 trillion.

The pattern around these events is well documented. Shares have often drifted lower into a launch and again just after it, then recovered over the following 30 to 60 days, a cycle Bank of America mapped across 24 iPhone launches dating back to 2007.

Related: Apple's new CEO inherits a fortune and an AI question

KeyBanc Capital Markets put a figure on the same tendency, finding that Apple stock has averaged a small decline on launch day over the past five years and a steeper one five sessions later, according to Investing.com.

That history carries more weight this year. John Ternus took over as CEO on Sept. 1, and the "Surprise and shine" event at Apple Park is his first, according to CNBC.

Bank of America keeps Apple's $380 target, with earnings 3% above consensus.Bloomberg / Getty Images
What Bank of America expects from the iPhone 18 lineup and the foldable

Bank of America analyst Wamsi Mohan kept a Buy rating and a $380 price objective in a note published Sept. 8.

Measured against the Sept. 8 close, that implies about 20% upside.

Mohan expects three phones on stage: the iPhone 18 Pro, the Pro Max, and Apple's first foldable, likely branded Ultra or Fold. He models price increases of $150 to $200 across the Pro line to absorb higher memory and storage costs, and points to media reports putting the foldable at $2,099, which would make it the most expensive iPhone the company has ever sold.

Here is what the bank is modeling, according to the note:

Fiscal 2026 revenue of $477 billion, up about 15% from a year earlier

Fiscal 2026 earnings of $8.85 a share, up roughly 19%

Fiscal 2027 earnings of $9.92 a share

September-quarter revenue of $112.7 billion and earnings of $1.97 a share

U.S. Bancorp To Launch Its Own Stablecoin

U.S. Bancorp (NYSE: $USB), the fifth largest lender in America, is preparing to launch its own stablecoin. 

The Minneapolis-based bank said that it has completed a live cross-border payment via the new stablecoin and is now weighing broader uses across its payments business.

The stablecoin is called USBDC (CRYPTO: $USBDC) and is pegged one-for-one to the U.S. dollar. The cross-border payment was completed between the U.S. and Europe, said the bank.

More From Cryptoprowl:

Bitmine Accelerates Ethereum Purchases To Close Out August

MEXC Data: BTC Breaks $80,000, Major-Asset Spot Trading Volume Surges 300%

The move by U.S. Bancorp comes as stablecoins tied to fiat money grow in popularity among traditional financial institutions. 

Dollar-pegged stablecoins are increasingly being used for payments, remittances, and treasury management, offering faster transaction speeds and around-the-clock settlement.

"This live pilot demonstrates our ability to accelerate global cash management and money movement capabilities," said U.S. Bancorp in a written statement. 

The lender added that it is exploring several uses for the new USBDC stablecoin, including cross-border treasury operations, liquidity management, and collateral movement. 

U.S. Bancorp did not say when the new stablecoin could become available to clients or give a timeline for a commercial rollout of the cryptocurrency.

News of U.S. Bancorp's stablecoin comes a week after 21 financial institutions, including Bank of America (NYSE: $BAC) and Goldman Sachs (NYSE: $GS), announced plans to form a company to issue stablecoins for payments and digital asset transactions. 

The consortium expects to introduce its first dollar-pegged stablecoin in 2027. 

USB stock has risen 27% over the last 12 months to trade at $62.49 U.S. per share.

title: Bank of America Is Bullish on SK hynix Stock as the Memory Chip Market Stays Tight
detail:
Bank of America Is Bullish on SK hynix Stock as the Memory Chip Market Stays Tight
Ian Cooper
Tue, September 8, 2026 at 10:36 AM CDT 4 min read
SKHY
BAC
Trade BAC on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
A concept image of space_ Image by Canities via Shutterstock_

SK hynix (SKHY) is starting to come back strong, especially with analysts at Bank of America out with a "Buy" rating and a $250 price target. In fact, analysts were far more bullish after a recent virtual memory tour, seeing tight memory supplies, strong demand for high-end chips, and more customers signing long-term deals as reasons for optimism.

Get exclusive insights with the FREE Barchart Brief newsletter. Subscribe now for quick, incisive midday market analysis you won't find anywhere else.

Memory Demand Isn't a Problem for SK hynix

Regarding the memory supply shortage, some companies are cutting back on the amount of memory they put into technology, such as PCs and smartphones. However, as analysts led by Simon Woo said, "de-spec [which means memory content cut per box or GPU/CPU] is mainly occurring in PCs/smartphones and low-end GPU/ASIC, but this should reflect memory chip shortages rather than demand cuts," as quoted by Seeking Alpha.

In short, the firm doesn't see demand dropping off. Instead, it's seeing companies using less memory in some technology because companies can't get enough supply. So, if SK hynix customers were cutting memory because consumers weren't buying technology, that would be bad news for SK hynix. But in this case, memory is being cut because supply is limited. Moreover, most of that impacts "lower-end products." With higher-end products, the analysts don't expect to see substantial cuts to memory at all. As also quoted by Seeking Alpha, the analysts said, "…high-end applications (including next-gen GPUs) will continue to use high memory content (no de-spec)." 

Supply Won't Catch Up to Demand Quick Enough

We also have to consider that a fresh supply of memory chips will not flood the market any time soon. According to SK hynix, the shortage could last until the end of 2030, with no real signs of substantial supply coming online any time soon. Bank of America says that space is limited, which means the industry can't simply flip a switch and dramatically increase production. That's still good news for SK hynix, though. That's because when there's strong demand and not enough supply, chipmakers have more room to keep prices and profit margins high.

In addition, SK hynix has reportedly extended its long-term deals. That's useful right now for the company, especially with tech giants needing substantial amounts of high-performance memory over the long haul.

Bank of America data shows 15-year-plus Treasuries just posted roughly -2% annualized returns over 10 years, the worst stretch since 1936.

While U.S. stocks returned 15% annually over the same period, TLT dropped over 26% from its early-2020 peak.

Rising yields that crushed existing bondholders now offer new buyers higher income and a stronger cushion against further rate increases.

Just released. Our analysts combed the entire stock market and named the ten best stocks to buy right now. The report is free. Enter your email and see if any of your stocks made the cut.

For years, bonds were treated as the portfolio ballast that investors could rely on when stocks stumbled. That assumption took a beating after 2020. The Federal Reserve's near-zero interest rates and quantitative easing pushed long-term Treasury yields to historic lows, leaving investors with little income and plenty of duration risk. When inflation returned, the setup reversed. 

Katiindies / Shutterstock.com

The Fed began aggressively raising interest rates in 2022, and long-duration bond prices fell as yields climbed. Now, Bank of America's latest data show just how unusual the damage has been: 15-year-plus U.S. Treasuries recently produced a roughly -2% annualized return over the previous 10 years, the worst reading in data going back to 1936.

How Treasuries Got Here

Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions. When yields rise, existing bonds paying lower coupons become less valuable.

That relationship became painful for investors who owned long-term Treasuries during the pandemic. Yields on long bonds fell toward 1% to 2% or lower, supported by Federal Reserve monetary policy and low inflation. They looked safe because the issuer was the U.S. government. But "safe" from default does not mean safe from falling prices.

Then, massive monetary stimulus, supply disruptions, and a reopening economy pushed inflation higher. The Fed responded with aggressive rate increases beginning in 2022. Higher yields translated into lower prices for existing long-duration bonds. The result was a rolling 10-year return that eventually slipped below zero.

title: BofA stays bullish on a cloud titan that is down 25%
detail:
BofA stays bullish on a cloud titan that is down 25%
Opeyemi Babalola
Mon, September 7, 2026 at 11:33 AM CDT 4 min read
BAC
ORCL
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Wall Street's two biggest markets are telling opposite stories about the same company right now. Equity investors keep buying every dip. Credit investors keep demanding more insurance against a default that stock buyers barely seem to consider.

Oracle Corporation (ORCL) sits at the center of that disagreement. Shares have fallen 25% since the company's last earnings report, yet BofA Securities is reiterating a Buy rating and a $240 price target ahead of Thursday's fiscal first-quarter results, according to the BofA note shared with TheStreet.

That target implies nearly 65% upside from current levels. BofA bases its $240 target on a 26.5x calendar-year 2027 earnings multiple, a notable premium over the broader software group's 19x average, arguing that rapid backlog conversion justifies the higher price tag.

This is not the first time Oracle's spending has spooked investors. Shares fell 11% in a single session in December 2025 after a smaller capex increase surprised the market, according to Fortune.

The pattern repeated in June 2026, when a bigger than expected capex figure triggered Oracle's steepest one day drop in six months, according to Bloomberg.

Related: BofA names 2 SpaceX alternatives with massive upside

The math behind BofA's confidence

BofA models cloud infrastructure revenue growing 116% year over year this quarter. That would push Oracle's total revenue growth to 28%, up from 21% in the prior quarter, as parts of Oracle's massive contract backlog begin converting into actual sales.

The acceleration matters because it would be the first hard evidence that Oracle's $638 billion backlog, the largest in enterprise software, is turning from promises into cash.

CNBC reported last week that Wall Street holds 42 buy ratings on the stock against just one sell heading into the print, with consensus estimates pointing to similarly steep growth.

Oracle's slower growing software business is quietly holding up too. BofA expects cloud applications revenue to grow 12.8% this quarter, accelerating from 10.3% in the prior period, while the database business keeps expanding into health care and other industry niches, according to the note.

That legacy engine gives Oracle a profitability cushion the AI infrastructure bet does not have on its own.

That growth is not free. BofA expects gross margin to slip to 63.8% and operating margin to 40%, down from 68.7% and 41.8% a year earlier, as the infrastructure business becomes a bigger share of revenue.

Faster growth and thinner margins are arriving together, which is exactly the tension investors are trying to price.

DBS, Citi Complete First Weekend Cross-Border Payment

DBS (SGX: D05) and Citi (NYSE: $C) have completed a cross-border US dollar payment between Singapore and the United States over the weekend, showing how tokenized bank deposits could help move money outside traditional banking hours.

The transaction was carried out on Saturday, September 5, between DBS in Singapore and Citi's New York office using tokenized deposits on Swift's Digital Ledger. The payment took minutes to settle, compared with the one to two business days that cross-border payments can take through traditional banking systems, the banks said in a Monday announcement.

The weekend transaction is the second confirmed live payment on Swift's blockchain-based ledger. HSBC and Standard Chartered completed the first in August, as Swift tests whether its infrastructure can support payments that run continuously rather than stopping around weekends and holidays.

Stablecoins and tokenized deposits allow value to move on digital networks around the clock, proving to be more efficient than the current banking system and forcing financial institutions to explore blockchain solutions to remain competitive.

DBS said 50% of finance leaders surveyed by the bank are exploring blockchain-based tools for liquidity and foreign-exchange management. Meanwhile, Asia's outbound cross-border payments are expected to reach $24 trillion by 2033, up from $13.5 trillion in 2025, according to figures cited by DBS from Money20/20 and FXC Intelligence.

Swift launched its blockchain ledger in July with 17 banks across six continents to connect existing banking infrastructure with newer digital payment networks.

In June, it was reported that JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: $JPM), Bank of America (NYSE: $BAC), and Citigroup (NYSE: C) are developing a shared tokenized deposit network that could launch by the first half of 2027 and be operated by The Clearing House. The system would turn traditional bank deposits into blockchain-based tokens, allowing faster transfers.

title: What's Powering Bank of America's Strong Capital Return Strategy?
detail:
What's Powering Bank of America's Strong Capital Return Strategy?
Nikita Kataruka
Mon, September 7, 2026 at 10:08 AM CDT 4 min read
BAC
JPM
MS-PQ
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Bank of America's BAC capital return story is supported by a combination of improving earnings power, a healthy capital cushion and disciplined balance-sheet management. After generating $30.5 billion in net income in 2025, the banking giant carried solid momentum into 2026. In the second quarter alone, net income reached $9.1 billion, while revenues rose 15% year over year to $31.6 billion. Net interest income (NII) rose 9%, while growth in trading, asset-management and investment banking (IB) fees further strengthened the company's earnings base.

BAC's capital position provides another important pillar for its shareholder-return strategy. At the end of June 2026, the company had $202 billion in CET1 capital, with its CET1 ratio holding at 11.2%. This remained comfortably above the 10% regulatory minimum. Further, the Federal Reserve's 2026 stress-test results left BAC's stress capital buffer at 2.5% through September 2027. This sizeable capital cushion gives management considerable flexibility to return excess capital while maintaining adequate buffers against potential economic and market volatility.

Share repurchases remain a central component of BAC's capital deployment strategy. The company's board authorized a $40-billion share repurchase program, effective Aug. 1, 2025. As of June 30, 2026, roughly $17 billion remained available under the program. This substantial capacity provides Bank of America with room to continue reducing its share count, which could support earnings over time.

Dividends complement these sizeable buybacks. Following the 2026 stress test, Bank of America raised its quarterly common stock dividend 14.3% to 32 cents per share, marking its sixth consecutive annual dividend hike. The increase underscores management's confidence in the company's earnings durability and capital-generation ability. More importantly, BAC has been able to increase shareholder payouts while continuing to invest across its businesses, demonstrating a balanced approach to growth and capital returns.

Overall, Bank of America appears well-positioned to sustain healthy capital distributions. Strong profitability, excess CET1 capital and considerable remaining buyback capacity provide a solid foundation for continued dividends and repurchases. While a higher G-SIB surcharge expected from January 2027 could modestly increase future capital requirements, continued NII growth, improving fee revenues and disciplined capital management should help offset some of that pressure.

BofA Sees Clear Winner Between Adobe and Oracle

This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

Adobe (NASDAQ:ADBE) and Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) report earnings on the same day, September 10, but Bank of America sees the two AI software giants moving in opposite directions.

Analyst Tal Liani maintained a Buy rating and $240 target on Oracle, implying 51% upside, while rating Adobe Sell with a $220 target, implying 17% downside. The contrast reflects one question: Which company is converting AI demand into meaningful financial growth?

ORCL GF Value chart

Wall Street expects Adobe's fiscal third-quarter earnings to reach $6.08 per share, up from $5.31, as revenue increases 11.7% to $6.69 billion. Those numbers are respectable, but BofA doubts AI is changing Adobe's growth trajectory.

Creative freemium monthly users reached 90 million, rising 70%, while AI-first annual recurring revenue exceeded $500 million, more than tripling. However, AI-first ARR remains below 2% of total ARR.

That gap explains why Liani calls Adobe's strategy largely defensive. AI tools may improve retention and engagement without generating substantial new revenue. BofA expects 11% ARR growth, or 9% excluding Semrush, while higher AI usage costs pressure margins.

Oracle's setup is more aggressive. Wall Street projects earnings of $1.74 per share, up 18.4%, and revenue of $19.13 billion, rising 28.1%. BofA expects infrastructure-as-a-service revenue to jump 116% as roughly one gigawatt of data-center capacity comes online.

Oracle also carries a $638 billion backlog. Yet that opportunity is expensive: BofA forecasts $21 billion in quarterly capital spending and $92.5 billion for the fiscal year. Oracle must prove cloud growth can outrun the resulting cash-flow strain.

Broader analyst sentiment supports the split. Adobe carries a Hold consensus with 1.43% downside, while Oracle has a Strong Buy consensus with 60.4% upside.

For investors, Adobe must show AI adoption accelerating monetization, while Oracle must demonstrate capital efficiency. BofA's preference is clear, but each company faces a different earnings test for shareholders on September 10.
